ai.definition: RegTech for AI refers to the application of technology, particularly artificial intelligence, to improve regulatory compliance and ethical standards in the development and deployment of AI systems.
ai.howItWorks: RegTech for AI tools leverage machine learning algorithms to monitor, analyze, and predict potential regulatory violations or ethical issues within an organization's AI operations. They can automate the process of identifying non-compliance with regulations, thereby reducing the risk of legal penalties and reputational damage.
ai.problemSolved: The primary problem addressed by RegTech for AI is ensuring that organizations adhere to relevant laws, guidelines, and ethical standards when developing and deploying AI systems, which can be complex and ever-evolving.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing processes are not directly applicable as this technology focuses on software and data analysis rather than physical products.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves the development of machine learning models that can interpret regulatory requirements, monitor AI system outputs for compliance, and generate alerts or recommendations when deviations occur. This includes data collection, model training, validation, and deployment.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the initial investment in developing and maintaining RegTech systems, ongoing data acquisition costs, and potential legal and reputational risks associated with non-compliance.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for this technology is positive as regulatory bodies increasingly demand greater transparency and accountability from AI deployments. However, the evolving nature of regulations poses challenges in maintaining up-to-date compliance solutions.
ai.regulation: RegTech for AI must comply with existing data protection laws (e.g., GDPR), industry-specific regulations, and emerging standards related to AI ethics and governance.
ai.risks: Risks include the potential for false positives or negatives in regulatory monitoring systems, the need for continuous updates to keep pace with changing regulations, and the challenge of integrating these tools into existing organizational processes.
ai.profitability: Profitability is driven by reducing legal risks, improving operational efficiency, and enhancing an organization's reputation. However, the initial investment required can be a barrier to entry.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on more sophisticated AI models that can better understand complex regulatory frameworks, as well as greater integration with existing compliance systems and increased automation of regulatory processes.

glossary.def: Technology used to improve regulatory compliance in various industries.
The study of ethical issues related to the development and use of artificial intelligence systems.
Adherence to laws, regulations, or standards set by governing bodies.

subsystems.name: Model and system inventory
subsystems.role: a live register of every AI system in use, who owns it and what it does.
parts: auto-discovery connectors to cloud and ML platforms

subsystems.name: Risk classification engine
subsystems.role: decides which rules apply to a given use case.

subsystems.name: Data governance and lineage
subsystems.role: tracks what data trained or drives each model, and whether its use is lawful.

subsystems.name: Testing and evaluation
subsystems.role: measures bias, accuracy, robustness and drift before and after deployment.

subsystems.name: Evidence and documentation
subsystems.role: produces the paperwork regulators and auditors expect.

subsystems.name: Runtime monitoring and incidents
subsystems.role: watches deployed models and routes problems to humans.

buildSteps.title: Translate rules into controls
buildSteps.detail: Legal text and standards such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework or ISO/IEC 42001 are broken into discrete, testable controls.

buildSteps.title: Connect to the estate
buildSteps.detail: Connectors read model registries, cloud accounts, code repositories and procurement records so systems are discovered automatically rather than self-reported.

buildSteps.title: Capture and classify each system
buildSteps.detail: Users record purpose, data, affected people and jurisdiction; the rules engine assigns a risk tier and the obligations that follow.

buildSteps.title: Automate evidence collection
buildSteps.detail: Scheduled jobs run bias, robustness and drift tests and store results with timestamps and model versions attached.

buildSteps.title: Generate documentation
buildSteps.detail: Templates are filled from the collected evidence to produce model cards, technical files and conformity declarations.

buildSteps.title: Monitor in production
buildSteps.detail: Live telemetry is checked against thresholds; breaches trigger alerts, human review and a recorded decision.

buildSteps.title: Expose an audit interface
buildSteps.detail: Dashboards and exportable, immutable evidence packs let internal auditors, customers or regulators inspect the trail.

buildSteps.title: Keep the rules current
buildSteps.detail: The control library is versioned and updated as regulations and harmonised standards change, so past assessments stay reproducible.

prerequisites.why: the EU AI Act set obligations that phase in from 2024, but the harmonised technical standards that make them checkable are still being written.

prerequisites.tech: Model registries and ML metadata tooling
prerequisites.why: compliance tools need a reliable list of models, versions and training runs to attach evidence to.
there is a working toolkit of statistical measures, though which ones satisfy a regulator is unsettled.
traceability across large training corpora is often incomplete, weakening any claim about lawful data use.
tools record decisions but cannot supply the accountable owner, review board or policy that regulation assumes.

pathway.milestone: firms build AI inventories and run voluntary assessments against frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF
pathway.unlocks: visibility of what AI is actually deployed.

pathway.milestone: high-risk obligations under the EU AI Act take effect and conformity assessment matures
pathway.unlocks: a genuine market for auditable compliance tooling.

pathway.milestone: AI governance platforms merge with model observability and security tooling
pathway.unlocks: one pipeline that tests, documents and monitors a model continuously.

pathway.milestone: regulator-facing reporting interfaces and mutual recognition between jurisdictions
pathway.unlocks: evidence produced once can satisfy multiple regulators, cutting duplicated audits.
